name: Denali Highway BLM Dispersed Primitive Camping (MP 79 Brushkana Corridor)

management_agency.name: Bureau of Land Management (BLM) - Glennallen Field Office

rules_and_regulations.cost: 100% Free - No fees, no permits required on BLM public lands
rules_and_regulations.stay_limit: 14 days maximum stay within any 28-day period
rules_and_regulations.guidelines: Dispersed camping is allowed on all unappropriated BLM public lands along the Denali Highway corridor. Pull off highway onto existing gravel turnouts. Do not create new tracks across tundra.

waste_disposal_rules.poop_disposal: In sub-arctic tundra, decomposition is extremely slow. Cat-holes must be 6-8 inches deep in topsoil, 200ft from water. Full pack-out of human waste using WAG bags is highly recommended due to fragile tundra and permafrost.
waste_disposal_rules.trash_policy: Strict LNT pack-it-in pack-it-out. Bears are highly active; zero food or trash may be left unsealed outside vehicles.

campfire_rules.firewood_policy: Dead/down spruce firewood gathering permitted. Tundra brush must not be cut or cleared.
campfire_rules.safety_requirements: Use existing rock/gravel fire rings. Ensure fires are completely extinguished with river water. Never ignite fires on organic peat/tundra moss (tundra fires burn underground).
campfire_rules.seasonal_fire_bans: Subject to Alaska Interagency Fire Center emergency burn bans during high wind and dry summer spells.

access_and_road_conditions.road_conditions: Rough gravel with sharp schist rocks, deep washboards, pot-holes, and dust clouds. Flat tires are extremely common.
access_and_road_conditions.vehicle_recommendation: High clearance car or 4x4 (Normal 2WD low-clearance cars can make it at slow speeds, but must carry 2 full-sized spare tires)

nomad_connectivity_rating.verizon_reliability: No service along vast stretches; spotty 1-bar 3G/LTE near Paxson or Cantwell ends
nomad_connectivity_rating.att_reliability: 1 bar Emergency 3G/LTE near high mountain passes
nomad_connectivity_rating.terrain_obstruction_risk: High (Alaska Range & Amphitheater Mountains block cellular signals; zero tower infrastructure)

amenities: Glacial River Water Access (Brushkana Creek / Delta River - heavy sediment filtering needed)

seasonal_weather_effects.spring: Late May thaw: heavy snowmelt, mud season, high flooding rivers, highway often closed until mid-May.
seasonal_weather_effects.summer: June-August: 20-24 hours daylight, 55-75°F, intense mosquito swarms, snow lingering on peaks.
seasonal_weather_effects.fall: Late August-September: Stunning golden tundra foliage, crisp 30-50°F, early night snow, Aurora Borealis viewing begins.
seasonal_weather_effects.winter: October-April: Extreme sub-zero arctic weather (-20 to -50°F), highway impassable and unmaintained.

dangers_and_hazards: Grizzly Bears (Ursus arctos horribilis) and Black Bears active throughout tundra; bear spray mandatory
Moose defense during spring calving and autumn rut
Remote isolation: no cellular service or tow trucks for 80+ miles
Sharp gravel rocks causing multiple tire punctures
Hypothermia risk even during summer cold rainstorms

common_human_made_sounds: Infrequent overlanding vehicle driving past on gravel highway (1 per hour in peak summer)

common_animals: Dall Sheep (Ovis dalli on high ridges)

human_demographics_and_culture: Off-grid arctic explorers, Starlink digital nomads, caribou hunters in autumn, overland expedition rigs, and berry pickers.

spiritual_and_folklore_data.nature_spirits_and_mythological_lore: Ahtna and Tanana Athabascan oral traditions honor the ancient mountain spirits of the Alaska Range and the sacred animal guardians of the caribou migration routes.
spiritual_and_folklore_data.energetic_and_spiritual_features: Profound arctic silence, raw glacial mountain energy, midnight sun solar saturation in summer, magnetic Aurora Borealis field in autumn nights.

nearby_hiking_trails.features: Tundra ridge walking, stream views, wildlife observation
Open alpine tundra, panoramic Alaska Range vistas

public_reviews_summary: One of the most spectacular sub-arctic boondocking drives on Earth. Total wilderness solitude. Starlink satellite internet is mandatory for remote work as cellular signal is non-existent.
other_data: Bortle Class 1 night sky (pristine zero light pollution). Aurora Borealis frequently visible starting in late August.
